endorsements.quote: To enhance trust, people should be made aware when AI or algorithms are being used in decision-making relating to their healthcare.
People must have a clear understanding of the purpose for which their data might be used and give consent for their data to be used in this way.

To help overcome barriers to uptake of AI health technologies, clinical trials of the technology should be co-designed with people with lived experience, and use relevant PROMs as a trial endpoint ( 43 ).
Advances in AI – whether relating to research, clinical practice or health systems policy - should not be developed in isolation and implemented ‘to’ people, but in collaboration ‘with’ them.

When developing models or interventions involving AI and PRO data, an essential consideration is that the data used to develop and train AI systems needs to be representative of the population in which the AI approach will be implemented.

unlisted_practices: Provide transparency about the data, instruments, and algorithms underlying AI, and about biases that may be inherent in programming and interpretation.
Do not prioritize AI-based predictions above patient experiential knowledge.
Use AI to complement rather than replace healthcare professionals.
Put safeguards in place for securely handling, storing, and using sensitive personal health data used by AI.
Conduct future research to determine whether AI used alongside standard of care improves outcomes such as disability and quality of life.
Pay particular attention to consent for people who may be experiencing cognitive dysfunction.
Design patient-reported data collection instruments so that people with cognitive dysfunction can complete them accurately.

screen.reason: This is a perspective article advocating for the incorporation of patient input and patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) when developing and implementing AI in healthcare, specifically for multiple sclerosis.
